title: Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion 6 months following atrial septal defect device closure: Has it eroded?
case_text:
A 41-year-old male manual laborer had presented with complaints of exertional dyspnea (New York Heart Association [NYHA] Functional Class II) of 1-year duration. He had a history of a serious road traffic accident that resulted in decreased movement of his right upper limb 4 years back. He also had a history of severe COVID-19 illness that required ventilatory care for 10 days in 2020. He was diagnosed with COVID-19-related lung fibrosis. He was being managed by a pulmonologist for the same and was prescribed inhaled steroids and bronchodilators. Cardiovascular evaluation was done for an incidentally detected murmur, which revealed an ostium secundum ASD. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed a large ostium secundum ASD (28 mm) shunting left to right with suitable rims but an absent aortic rim. X-ray and computerized tomography (CT) thorax revealed COVID-19-related extensive fibrosis of the right lung and an elevated right diaphragm. On fluoroscopy, the right hemidiaphragm moved paradoxically during the sniff test. There was no resting hypoxia/hypercapnia, and lung function tests showed moderate restrictive physiology. Considering his multiple comorbid conditions, he underwent a cardiac catheterization that revealed a Qp/Qs of 3:1, mean pulmonary artery pressure of 25 mmHg, and normal coronaries. After a thorough evaluation and discussion with the pulmonologist and cardiac surgeon, a decision to close the ASD with a device was made.
He underwent ASD closure with a 32-mm Atrial Septal Occluder (ASO) device (Abbot Cardiovascular Plymouth MN) under TEE guidance. There were no periprocedural complications. At discharge, he was prescribed aspirin and clopidogrel for 6 months. He remained asymptomatic for 4 months postdevice closure. His routine echocardiography performed 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months following the procedure showed a typically positioned device with no other complications. He resumed all his physical activities and was symptom-free.
He started experiencing exertional dyspnea NYHA Class II for 2 weeks following a brief febrile illness. He had worsening shortness of breath (NYHA IV) with one episode of syncope, for which he was evaluated at a facility in his hometown. The treating cardiologist made a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade, and nearly 700-800 mL of hemorrhagic pericardial fluid was drained. He was medically stabilized and was referred to our center. Pericardial fluid workup revealed a white blood cell count of 10/mm3 with predominant lymphocytes, red blood cell count of 8640/mm3, exudative effusion with 6.86 g/dL protein, and a borderline elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA) of 31 U/L. His inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate - 56 mm/h and C reactive protein - 15 mg/L) were elevated. Suspecting ASD device erosion, several investigations were carried out.
TEE [Figures 1 and 2] showed an ASD device in situ with minimal pericardial effusion (~4 mm) and no definite evidence of aortic or atrial wall erosion. CT angiography failed to reveal definite evidence of device erosion. The pericardium was slightly thickened and enhanced [Figures 3 and 4a-d].
Positron emission tomography (PET)-CT showed an intense fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the ASD device [Figure 5]. Hence, a diagnosis of device infection was suspected. The dilemma persisted! Repeated blood cultures, including fungal cultures, were sterile. A careful reanalysis of the history revealed a history of rising evening temperatures, and a tuberculin test was strongly positive. CT thorax also revealed a few significant matted lymph nodes in the mediastinum, which were new changes compared to the pre-ASD device closure CT images. The extent of lung fibrosis on the CT scan remained the same. Given the high endemicity of tuberculosis in India, the patient was started on antitubercular therapy. Subsequent TTEs showed no increase in effusion, and the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Follow-up at 6 months and 1 year showed no recurrence of pericardial effusion.

   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
